teaser.text: Coca-Cola HBC is the local manufacturer, seller and distributor of branded drinks across Europe and Africa. Its business is to turn powerful brands, factories and delivery networks into sales to shops, restaurants and other outlets.

blocks.heading: Where could Coca-Cola HBC's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The probability-weighted price is 4106.03 GBp in October 2027, a 5% loss including dividends. It reaches 4311.87 GBp in October 2028, a 3% gain. By October 2029, it reaches 4632.79 GBp, a 13% gain. The 2029 range runs from 2708.85 GBp in the bear case to 6800.11 GBp in the bull case, so execution matters more than the central estimate suggests.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Coca-Cola HBC, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: Base earnings rise from €1,173.9 million in October 2027 to €1,362 million in October 2029. The starting point is close to the analyst next-twelve-month estimate, which implies about €1,170.5 million on the forecast share count. The latest half-year supports the anchor: revenue and net income both increased year on year. The bear row declines as currency, financing and integration pressure erode margins, while the bull row accelerates on sustained volume growth and operating leverage. H1 organic cases grew 7.5%, including 26.1% growth in energy, but free cash flow fell, so stronger demand is not yet equivalent to stronger cash generation.

The bull case reaches 4838.10 GBp first and 6800.11 GBp last, with an 18% probability. It needs sustained energy and market-share gains, better utilisation, successful CCBA integration, stronger cash conversion and renewed buybacks. The volume evidence supports possibility, but the cash-flow decline makes this alignment less likely.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Coca-Cola HBC really make?

paragraphs.text: In 2025, capital spending, lease payments and interest absorbed much of the operating cash. Stock-based pay reduced the economic remainder further because employee awards give staff a claim on future shareholder value, even though they do not consume the same cash immediately.

Management reported €700.0 million of its own free cash flow. Its bridge uses different deductions and changed in 2025 to add acquisition costs back into operating cash. That makes the measure useful as management’s view, but less useful for an unchanged comparison across years. The specialist keeps one consistent bridge and treats the company’s figure as a second lens.

blocks.heading: How much does Coca-Cola HBC pay in dividends over time?

paragraphs.text: Base dividends increase from €1.32 to €1.58 per share. The path follows HBC’s progressive policy and its recent 44% payout, while allowing investment and financing needs to absorb some cash. The bear case holds the latest €1.20 dividend for two periods before a small recovery; the bull case reaches €1.85 as earnings and cash conversion improve. The latest payment was €1.20, but free cash flow weakened in 2025 and again in the first half of 2026.

blocks.heading: What could change Coca-Cola HBC's dividend?

paragraphs.text: The view would move toward the bear case if CCBA completion or integration disappoints during 2027–28, if net debt rises while EPS and free cash flow fall, or if currencies and trapped Russian cash reduce reported earnings through 2029. Capacity and input costs exceeding profitable volume would add another downside signal.

blocks.heading: What is Coca-Cola HBC's dividend yield against its price?

paragraphs.text: EBITDA means earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. It helps compare operating businesses, but it is not cash. A bottler needs factories, trucks and café coolers; depreciation records the use of those assets, while cash is needed later to replace them. CCH generated €700.0 million of free cash flow in 2025, while capital expenditure was €827.6 million. The cash-flow and dividend yields therefore need to be judged against several years of investment, not one period.
